## Another route in: `skill-dev`

`skill-dev` opens installed **skills and plugins** in project-local worktrees
(`skill-dev open <plugin>` → edit → `close --merge`), so it is a second way a
consumer-side edit reaches the store copy — with the same consequence as flow E
and one difference: it merges back rather than opening a PR. Everything above
about propagation applies unchanged; the edit is in the plugin repo and nowhere
else until flow C runs. Use `skill-dev` for a deliberate editing session on the
bundle, `skt publish` for an edit you already made in a home.

## The integrating agent

The loop that becomes possible once bundles exist. Give an agent the plugin
repos and their upstream skill repos, and have it run:

1. **Watch.** For each bundle, which constituents' remotes are ahead of the
   parent's copy? (`git -C skills/<n> fetch && git -C skills/<n> rev-list --count HEAD..origin/<b>`)
2. **Judge coherence.** Do the pending upstream changes across the bundle *fit
   together*, and with what consumers currently expect? A rename that landed in
   one skill and not its caller is a reason to wait, not to pull.
3. **Pull and cut** — flow A — when they do, one PR, one version.
4. **Sweep the other direction.** Any skill edits sitting in a plugin repo
   unpropagated (flow E)? Fan them out — flow C.
5. **Report.** Which bundles moved, which consumers should sync, what was held
   back and why.

Step 2 is the judgment that has no home under one-repo-per-skill: there, every
skill publishes independently and "when does this reach consumers" is decided by
whenever each consumer happens to sync. Here it is a decision with an owner.

1	# Per-checkout Skill Manager homes
2	
3	**This page and the scripts it documents belong to `git-issue-workflow`.** A home
4	is a fact about a CHECKOUT, and every repo has checkouts; only some repos have
5	constituents. It used to live in `git-integration-repo`, which meant an agent
6	working a plain repo — reading that skill's description and correctly concluding
7	it was irrelevant — never found it. The integration-repo sections below are still
8	here because an integration repo is one of the shapes a checkout comes in, not
9	because the mechanism is integration-specific.
10	
11	An agent working a ticket installs, edits, syncs and binds skills. By default all
12	of that lands in the operator's global `~/.skill-manager`, which every other
13	agent and every other worktree is also using. Parallel tickets collide there, and
14	an improvement an agent makes to a skill has no defined route back to that
15	skill's own repo.
16	
17	So each checkout gets its **own** home:
18	
19	```
20	<checkout>/.skill-manager/        the home (a clone of an existing home)
21	<checkout>/.skill-manager/home.runtime.json    the launch descriptor
22	<checkout>/.skill-manager/home.policy.toml     live | frozen
23	<checkout>/.skill-manager/bin/launch/{claude,codex,gemini}   launcher shims
24	<checkout>/.claude  <checkout>/.codex  <checkout>/.gemini    agent homes
25	```
26	
27	One script does this, for both the repo root and every worktree:
28	
29	```bash
30	"${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/bootstrap-home.sh" --root <checkout>
31	```
32	
33	**An agent does not need that path memorised, and does not need a copy of
34	anything.** `wt new` in a repository with no home yet exits 3 and prints the
35	line above with both paths already absolute; running it verbatim is the whole
36	onboarding. So no repo is *required* to carry a locator, and copying one in is
37	not a prerequisite for anything.
38	
39	A repo *may* additionally carry `scripts/agent-home.sh`, purely so a human in
40	the checkout can type `scripts/agent-home.sh` instead of the long path. **This
41	skill ships that file**: copy
42	`${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/agent-home.sh`
43	into the target repo's own `scripts/` directory. It holds no policy — it finds
44	the `bootstrap-home.sh` above and `exec`s it with `--root <repo>`, so a copy of
45	it is never a copy of the ordering rules. It is a convenience, not a rung the
46	mechanism depends on; a consumer that never copies it loses nothing.
47	
48	**Which copy it found is printed on every run**, because "the bootstrap ran" and
49	"the bootstrap you reviewed ran" are different facts. Measured, same fixture,
50	same command: the checkout's copy projected 18 of 18 skills into every agent
51	home, and `~/.skill-manager`'s copy — 33 KB, predating the projection work —
52	produced **empty agent homes** and exited 0. So the locator does not accept a
53	candidate because the file exists. It asks each one whether `--help` names
54	`--allow-unprojected`, the flag that arrived with projection support, skips the
55	ones that cannot answer, and **refuses** (naming every candidate and its
56	verdict) if none can. The remedy it prints is `skill-manager sync`, or
57	`INTEGRATION_BOOTSTRAP_HOME=<path>/scripts/bootstrap-home.sh`, which is to this
58	skill's *scripts* what `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI` is to the CLI: the only way to pin
59	which copy runs. Nothing else pins them — an installed unit's scripts come from
60	whichever home resolved it, and that home can be arbitrarily stale (measured
61	skew on one machine: checkout `941ec20`, `~/.skill-manager` `c5abdab`, project
62	home `24fe6e8`).
63	
64	## Where the isolation actually comes from
65	
66	`SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` alone is **not** enough, and assuming it is has cost this
67	epic real time:
68	
69	- Skills load from Claude's config dir, so `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (and
70	  `CLAUDE_HOME`, which carries the same value) must be redirected too. Both are
71	  emitted by the descriptor; `skill-manager exec` refuses a launch where they
72	  still resolve outside the home.
73	- `skill-script` CLI deps are generated shell scripts with a home's absolute
74	  path in the body. No variable redirects those, so the launch PATH puts this
75	  home's `bin/` first **and removes other homes' `bin/`**.
76	
77	All of that lives in `skill-manager exec` / `LaunchEnv`. The generated shims are
78	thin wrappers over it. **Launch agents through the shims** (or through
79	`skill-manager exec`) and you inherit the whole contract; export variables by
80	hand and you get the part you remembered.
81	
82	### It is a convention, and it is enforced by tests rather than by the kernel
83	
84	Say what that is plainly: **env vars and PATH order**. Nothing in it *stops* a
85	process writing to `~/.skill-manager`, to another project's home, or to
86	`~/.ssh`. A determined — or merely surprising — process can write anywhere the
87	operator can. Every leak this epic fixed was a process writing where nothing
88	stopped it.
89	
90	What keeps the convention from regressing is not a boundary, it is that the
91	recipe is written down **once** and something fails when a second copy appears:
92	
93	- `test_graph/sources/lib/SmEnv.java` in `skill-manager` is the only place that
94	  puts `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME`, `SKILL_MANAGER_INSTALL_DIR`, `CLAUDE_HOME`,
95	  `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME` or `GEMINI_HOME` into a child environment.
96	  `sources/sandbox/SandboxEnvContract.java` is the oracle that keeps it the only
97	  one: it fails if any other file writes one of those, and it fails if a file
98	  that spawns the CLI does not reach `SmEnv` through its own `//SOURCES`
99	  closure. It plants five synthetic nodes every run and requires the detector to
100	  flag three and clear two, because a scan reporting "no violations" is worth
101	  nothing until it has been shown to report one. Before that existed the recipe
102	  lived in prose and four disagreeing copies, and **50 of 105** CLI env sites
103	  passed neither the agent variables nor `HOME` — one of those projections
104	  turned up in a live agent's available-skills list. It is 0 now.
105	- `LaunchEnv.requireClaudeRedirected()`, called by `ExecCommand` **before any
106	  child process is created**, refuses a launch whose Claude config directory
107	  resolves outside the home root. Skills load from that directory, so an
108	  unredirected one is not a warning, it is the wrong home.
109	
110	A `sandbox-exec` (Seatbelt) layer was built to make this a real kernel boundary,
111	and it was **removed** (`skill-manager` #60, closed as not-planned; commit
112	`5f8d61e`). Three reasons, none of them a defect in the code: it is macOS-only,
113	so the guarantee existed on one platform and every other got the convention
114	anyway; it fought the harnesses it was protecting, because `claude` and `codex`
115	each spawn their own tooling and each met the profile somewhere different, so
116	the failure mode was a mid-session `EPERM` from a process skill-manager did not
117	write and could not explain; and its cache redirection gave every home a private
118	copy of stores the operator already had (`~/.cache/uv` alone is 51 GB here, and
119	this machine carries 35 homes). If you are looking for `SKILL_MANAGER_SANDBOX`,
120	`launch.sb` or `home shims --sandbox`: they do not exist. Nothing in this repo
121	offers a kernel boundary, and an earlier version of this page said otherwise.
122	
123	### What a per-home clone actually costs
124	
125	The three-tier model — a home per repository, a home per ticket worktree — is
126	affordable because a clone is **copy-on-write**, not a copy. `Files.copy` with
127	`COPY_ATTRIBUTES` takes the JDK's `clonefile(2)` path on APFS and the
128	destination shares the source's blocks. Measured on this host by free-space
129	delta on a dedicated volume: a `home clone` of a 189 MB home consumes **7.22 MB
130	— 3.8%**. Do not check this with `du`; it attributes shared blocks to both files
131	and reported 197.1 MB against 7.14 MB real.
132	
133	`cache/`, `tmp/`, `logs/`, `venvs/`, `tools/` and `npm/` are skipped on top of
134	that (see the clone caveat further down).
135	
136	### Package caches are shared; install targets are not
137	
138	A home does **not** get a private package cache, and the distinction is not
139	read-only versus writable — nothing here is read-only, and an agent can still
140	`uv pip install` (`skill-manager` commit `8fddd6e`, `pm/PackageCaches.java`):
141	
142	| | category | |
143	|---|---|---|
144	| `~/.cache/uv`, `~/.npm`, the pip wheel cache | content-addressed | **shared** — an entry is named by the hash of what it holds, so two homes racing to populate one key write the same bytes |
145	| `<home>/venvs`, `<home>/bin/cli`, `<home>/npm/<skill>`, `<home>/pm/<tool>`, `<home>/cache` | install target | **per-home** — mutable, and two homes pointed at one are a `--force` away from pulling the interpreter out from under each other |
146	
147	Sharing the store only pays if materializing out of it is cheap, so `UV_LINK_MODE`
148	is chosen per filesystem: `clone` (reflink) when the store and the home can
149	share blocks, `hardlink` on a same-filesystem pair that cannot reflink, `copy`
150	across filesystems. Guessing wrong degrades rather than breaks — uv falls back
151	to copy and warns. Measured counter-example for why this matters: three
152	skill-script venvs in one home held 48,258 files across 48,258 distinct inodes,
153	1.6 GB with zero sharing.
154	
155	## When to bootstrap
156	
157	| Checkout | When | How |
158	|---|---|---|
159	| Repo root (the main tree, where constituent `.git`s live) | Once, at onboarding, and again after the home is deleted | `scripts/agent-home.sh` |
160	| A ticket worktree | Automatically, by `new-change.sh`, before it returns | nothing to do |
161	| A worktree made by hand (`git worktree add`) | Immediately after creating it | `bootstrap-home.sh --root <wt>` |
162	| A **nested** integration repo (a constituent that is itself one) | At its own root, as its own checkout | `bootstrap-home.sh --root constituents/<nested>` |
163	| A constituent you are working in directly | Only if you run an agent from inside it rather than from the parent | `bootstrap-home.sh --root constituents/<name>` |
164	
165	`bootstrap-home.sh` with no `--root` defaults to the **nearest enclosing git
166	toplevel**, which inside `constituents/deploy-helm` is deploy-helm — not the
167	integration parent. It used to walk up to `integration.toml` instead, so a bare
168	run from a constituent reported on (or created) the *parent's* home; usually the
169	parent's home already existed, so the run just said "already bootstrapped" and
170	the operator learned nothing.
171	
172	A nested integration repo is not special-cased: it bootstraps at its own root
173	because that is the checkout an agent works in. Leaf-first ordering still
174	applies to *content* — a change to a leaf that the nested parent also contains
175	starts in the leaf, not in the duplicated nested path — and having a home per
176	checkout does not change that ordering at all.
177	
178	## Which home a bootstrap clones FROM — and why it is not a choice
179	
180	A worktree home and the project home it will be reconciled back into must be
181	**the same pair by construction**. `bootstrap-home.sh` and `close-change.sh`
182	both derive it from the checkout, through one function (`project_home` in
183	`lib.sh`):
184	
185	| Checkout being bootstrapped | Cloned from | `close-change.sh --into` |
186	|---|---|---|
187	| A **linked worktree** | its project home — `<main working tree>/.skill-manager` | the same path |
188	| A **main working tree** | `$SKILL_MANAGER_HOME`, else `~/.skill-manager` | n/a — nothing closes it out |
189	
190	`$SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` is **not** consulted for a worktree, deliberately. It used
191	to be the default for both tiers while `close-change.sh` defaulted `--into` to
192	`<repo-root>/.skill-manager`, and from a **bare shell** those name different
193	homes: measured, bootstrap cloned the operator's 845 MB global home into the
194	worktree and `home close-out` then blocked on **17 units before any work
195	existed**, printing a remedy that would have synced those global units *into*
196	the project home. The launch shims export `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` and so never met
197	it; a human running the scripts by hand did (issue #50).
198	
199	Two things therefore **refuse** rather than fall back:
200	
201	- a worktree whose project has **no home yet** — bootstrap it at the project
202	  first, because a home cloned from anywhere else cannot be closed into the
203	  project;
204	- an explicit `--source` that is not the project home.
205	
206	When the bootstrap refuses, `new-change.sh` **rolls the worktree and its branch
207	back**, so the operator's next command is the one the message names rather than
208	`worktree path already exists`.
209	
210	`scripts/selftest.sh` proves both directions on a disposable fixture, from a
211	bare shell, against a decoy global home: it asserts by **unit name present /
212	absent** which home the worktree's copy came from, so a check that only looked
213	for the right unit could not pass a home that carried both. It also pins the
214	things that have no other coverage — that a ticket resolves to the same worktree
215	from a sibling worktree, that `--dry-run` from *inside* a worktree is answered
216	while a real removal from inside it refuses, that a refused bootstrap leaves no
217	worktree or branch behind, and that a remedy's conflicted-file list is not
218	mangled.
219	
220	## Which `skill-manager` a home uses
221	
222	`home clone`, `home shims`, `home policy`, `home describe` and `exec` are newer
223	than the released CLI, so `bootstrap-home.sh` probes for a build that has them:
224	`SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`, then `PATH`, then a `skill-manager` the checkout itself
225	ships, then one the **enclosing integration repo** ships. That last entry is
226	what lets a constituent home find a capable build at all: bootstrapping
227	`constituents/deploy-helm` searched only deploy-helm, which ships no CLI, so it
228	either refused or ran on a `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI` the caller exported by hand and
229	that nothing recorded. The epic build lives in the parent. If nothing answers
230	`home clone`, it refuses **before** creating anything and tells you why — a
231	half-bootstrapped worktree is worse than none.
232	
233	### The pin at `<home>/bin/cli/skill-manager`
234	
235	That slot decides which build every launch from the home runs. The generated
236	launchers read it and `HomeDescriptor.resolveCli` documents it as rule 3, and
237	since `skill-manager` issue #61 there is **no `PATH` fallback behind it** — the
238	launcher's last line is `exec "$cli" exec --home …` and the released 0.19.2 on
239	`PATH` has no `exec` subcommand, so a `PATH` branch could only ever produce
240	`Unmatched arguments: 'exec'`. A wrong or missing pin is therefore not a
241	downgrade, it is a home that cannot launch.
242	
243	**`skill-manager home shims` writes it. `bootstrap-home.sh` does not.**
244	
245	It used to, and that was right at the time: `home shims` wrote a
246	`PATH`-resolving shim, so homes bootstrapped through this script worked and
247	homes provisioned by `home shims` alone died at their last line — and because
248	this script masked the difference across a 24-repo onboarding fan-out, nobody
249	saw it. Commit `e65962e` fixed `home shims` to write the absolute pin itself,
250	derived from the build running it (`RunningCli`), and at that moment two writers
251	of one file stopped being a redundancy and became a race with one correct
252	answer.
253	
254	This script's predicate lost that race. It decided whether to overwrite by
255	grepping the slot for the literal words `home shims` — which the **fixed**
256	generated file also contains. Measured: **17 of 25** homes had a correct pin
257	replaced by a pin to whatever `pick_cli` had chosen, and an 18th, written before
258	the script marked its own output, was not repaired at all. A predicate that keys
259	on prose cannot distinguish versions of the prose, which is why the fix
260	introduced a stable token — `skill-manager:cli-pin`, `LauncherShims.PIN_MARKER`,
261	on line 2 of the generated body.
262	
263	So `ensure_cli_pin` **verifies, and delegates every repair to the one writer**:
264	
265	| What is in the slot | What happens |
266	|---|---|
267	| The `skill-manager:cli-pin` marker | Read the pinned path, check it is executable, **stop**. The file is not this script's to rewrite. |
268	| Nothing | Re-run `home shims` |
269	| This script's own older pin (`git-integration-repo:cli-pin`, or the unmarked one before it) | Re-run `home shims` |
270	| A pre-#61 `PATH`-resolving shim (identified by its `command -v skill-manager`, since it carries no marker) | Re-run `home shims` |
271	| Anything else | Left alone — it could be a real CLI dep |
272	
273	A pin whose target is **gone** is a refusal, not a repair: the script names the
274	missing path and the command that re-pins it (`home shims --home <store>`, run
275	from the build the home should use) and writes nothing. Substituting a CLI of
276	its own choosing is exactly what overwrote the 17.
277	
278	This runs on an already-bootstrapped home without `--force`, because the
279	operator has no way to know the slot is wrong. A **frozen** home is never
280	written, here as everywhere else.
281	
282	`home shims` itself **refuses rather than guessing**: `RunningCli` probes
283	`SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`, the running process's own command,
284	`SKILL_MANAGER_INSTALL_DIR` and the jar's location, and exits 127 having written
285	nothing when none answers. Every candidate `pick_cli` can return is a launcher
286	that exports `SKILL_MANAGER_INSTALL_DIR` before it execs the JVM, so the probe
287	succeeds — but `bootstrap-home.sh` prints that refusal verbatim rather than
288	reducing it to an exit code, because a `$CLI` that is not a launcher (a bare
289	`jbang SkillManager.java`) is a configuration mistake that deserves the CLI's
290	own diagnostic.
291	
292	Pinning the slot does **not** retire `close-change.sh`'s help-**text** probe.
293	`pick_cli` still consults `PATH` when nothing else answers. From a bare shell
294	that is the released 0.19.2, so the exit-status trap is still reachable; from
295	inside an agent session it is *another home's pin*, because `skill-manager exec`
296	puts `<home>/bin/cli` first on the launch `PATH`.
297	
298	#### The pin resolves itself through `$SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`, so do not point that at it
299	
300	The generated body is `cli="${SKILL_MANAGER_CLI:-<absolute>}"` followed by
301	`exec "$cli" "$@"`. The variable is honoured **first** so a harness can redirect
302	the pin at a build of its own; the absolute default is what makes the pin a pin.
303	Naming the pin itself in that variable therefore throws away the target it
304	already knows and replaces it with a path to itself, and it re-execs **forever**
305	— no output, no exit, one process burning a core.
306	
307	This is not hypothetical and it is not a corner: `pick_cli` in both
308	`bootstrap-home.sh` and `close-change.sh` *prefers* the home's own pin, and
309	`exec` puts a pin first on an agent session's `PATH`, so "the CLI I picked" and
310	"the CLI that must not be named in that variable" are usually the same file.
311	`close-change.sh` shipped exactly that pairing for one epic; see
312	[Teardown](#teardown-including-at-epic-close).
313	
314	Rules for anything that invokes a chosen CLI:
315	
316	- Decide **per candidate**. The variable is still what makes a remedy printed by
317	  a non-self-pinning launcher name a runnable path.
318	- **Scrub an inherited value**, do not merely refrain from setting one. The
319	  livelock does not care who exported it.
320	- Do not assume a candidate is safe because it came from `PATH`, and do not
321	  identify the hazard by path alone — inside an agent session the `PATH` answer
322	  is a pin belonging to a home the caller has never heard of. The reliable
323	  predicate is the candidate's own bytes: does it *expand*
324	  `$SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`?
325	- Do not rely on the CLI to defend itself. A guard added to the shim today is
326	  absent from every home already pinned by an older build, which is most of the
327	  homes a teardown will ever meet.
328	
329	## The one ordering rule
330	
331	```
332	clone the home  ->  point SKILL_MANAGER_HOME at the clone  ->  everything else
333	```
334	
335	`install`, `sync`, `bind`, `upgrade` and `project resolve` all write into
336	whatever `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` names, and `project resolve` additionally writes a
337	child-home record and a projection ledger into that store. Run any of them
338	before the local home exists and they mutate the operator's global home. That is
339	why `bootstrap-home.sh` clones as its first command, exports
340	`SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` as its second, and re-asserts the export before every
341	mutating step. Do not reproduce the sequence by hand.
342	
343	Two consequences worth stating:
344	
345	- **A cloned home is not a `project resolve` child home.** Both want the path
346	  `<root>/.skill-manager`. Resolving a root against that root's own home makes
347	  the home its own child: measured, it exits 0 and destroys nothing (unit
348	  materialization no-ops when source and destination are the same real path),
349	  but it records a child home whose parent and child are one directory and it
350	  isolates nothing. Pick the clone for a checkout an agent works in; use
351	  `project resolve` when the parent home lives somewhere else. Either way,
352	  never resolve before the local home exists — that is the case where the
353	  child-home record and the ledger land in the operator's global home.
354	- **A clone is not a full copy, and that is the design, not a shortfall.**
355	  `cache/`, `tmp/`, `logs/`, `venvs/`, `tools/` and `npm/` are skipped (they are
356	  re-derivable, and copying `tools/` costs 1.3 GB). **`pm/` is deliberately NOT
357	  in that list** — it holds the pinned package managers, and a home that cannot
358	  run `uv` cannot rebuild anything. What the clone does with the
359	  artifacts under those roots — and what you should do about it, which is
360	  usually nothing — **is stated once and is not repeated here:**
361	  `${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/plugins/skt/skills/skt/references/derived-artifacts.md` (absent in a home that does not have the skt plugin installed). Read it before concluding a fresh worktree home is damaged.
362	
363	  Two things this page still owns, both measured:
364	  - Run any `sync` with the **agent-home variables set**, not with
365	    `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` alone. `sync` ends in a binding step, and with
366	    `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME` and `GEMINI_HOME` unset that step writes
367	    the operator's `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml` and
368	    `~/.gemini/settings.json` (`ADDED claude (~/.claude.json)` —
369	    skill-manager#145). `bootstrap-home.sh` prints the safe spelling; the line
370	    `home clone` itself prints is the unsafe one.
371	  - **This page used to say `home verify` refuses a clone until those links are
372	    re-provisioned, and that `sync` could not do it — "a skill-manager gap".
373	    RETRACTED: re-measured 2026-08-23, a fresh ticket-worktree clone passes
374	    `skill-manager home verify` (exit 0) untouched.** The claim is left here as
375	    a correction so nobody restores it from memory. Why it is no longer true,
376	    and what the states actually are, is the artifact page above — this bullet
377	    deliberately does not reproduce its details. **Do not chase `home verify` to
378	    a green it already has.**
379	
380	    A link that *genuinely* does not resolve is a different thing and **is**
381	    still refused (exit 1, measured the same day) — see the next bullet.
382	
383	- **A clone of an empty home is an empty home** (git-integration-skill#10).
384	  Cloning copies units; it never *installs* any. A source home holding no skills
385	  therefore yields a perfectly well-formed home — right descriptor, right policy,
386	  working shims, happy `exec --print-env` — that serves an agent **zero skills**.
387	  The step that installs the bundled ones is `skill-manager onboard`, and it is
388	  not part of the clone.
389	
390	  `bootstrap-home.sh` **refuses** such a home (exit `5`) rather than reporting it
391	  verified, and names `onboard`. It refuses rather than running it because
392	  `onboard` clones from github and touches the gateway, which is a contended
393	  singleton (skill-manager#132) — too expensive to attach to the most repeated
394	  command in this repo. Pass `--onboard` to have it run
395	  `onboard --skip-gateway` for you, `--onboard-gateway` to include the gateway,
396	  or `--allow-empty` to accept an empty home deliberately.

398	  For a **worktree** the remedy is always the *project* home, and `--onboard` is
399	  refused outright there: a worktree home is a copy of the project home and
400	  `close-change.sh` reconciles it back into that same home, so units installed
401	  into the copy are units the project never had — every one of them a teardown
402	  blocker before any work exists (issue #50).
403	
404	- **A home full of skills is not a home an agent can read them from.** The store
405	  is `<home>/skills/`. *No agent reads it.* An agent reads
406	  `<root>/.claude/skills/<unit>` and its `.codex` / `.gemini` siblings, which are
407	  symlinks into the store, recorded in `installed/<unit>.projections.json` as
408	  `default:<agent>:<unit>` bindings.
409	
410	  `home clone` copies the **store**. The agent homes live *beside* it, so they
411	  are not in the copy — and a freshly cloned worktree home therefore has a full
412	  store and three empty agent directories. Measured: `wt new`, exit 0, full
413	  contract, `verified: 20 skill(s) servable`, and `ls -a <wt>/.claude` answering
414	  `.` and `..`. Every agent launched in that worktree saw **zero** skills.
415	  `skill-manager exec` reports it on every launch — one `! reconcile: no
416	  skill-manager projection for <u> on <agent> at <path>` line per missing
417	  link — and creates nothing.
418	
419	  `bootstrap-home.sh` now fixes it, and the order it fixes it in matters:
420	
421	  1. **From the home's own ledger.** `home clone` copies
422	     `installed/<unit>.projections.json` *and re-anchors it*, so a fresh
423	     worktree home already declares the right destination under the right root.
424	     The records are correct; only the symlinks are missing. Materializing them
425	     is instant, offline, and touches no unit content.
426	  2. **`sync --skip-mcp`, only for what the ledger cannot answer** — a unit with
427	     no binding record at all, which is what a scaffolded or hand-seeded home
428	     has.
429	
430	  That order is not a preference. `sync` refreshes unit *content*: measured on a
431	  worktree whose home was a correct copy of a complete project home, projecting
432	  through `sync` left `skills/<unit>/.git/index` differing from the project
433	  home's and `home close-out` then **refused the teardown** — issue #50
434	  reintroduced by the fix for this. With the ledger step first the same worktree
435	  needs no sync at all and closes cleanly.

437	  The run then reports `projected: N of M into each of .claude .codex .gemini`,
438	  and prints `verified:` **only when N = M**. A home an agent cannot read its
439	  skills from exits `6` and names every missing link plus the `sync --skip-mcp`
440	  that would create it; `--allow-unprojected` accepts one deliberately (still
441	  never as *verified*), and `--no-project` skips the projection step entirely.

499	## The first launch is gated on change awareness (exit 8)
500	
501	A bootstrapped home is not the same thing as a home you can launch from. There
502	is one more gate, it belongs to `skill-manager` rather than to these scripts,
503	and **it is the first thing an operator meets after `new-change.sh` returns**.
504	
505	### What it is for
506	
507	An agent reads a skill, then works for twenty minutes on the strength of it. A
508	sync, a pull, or a fresh clone replaces that skill underneath it. Nothing fails
509	and nothing warns, and the agent keeps following instructions that no longer
510	exist. The only boundary at which that can still be said out loud is between
511	"the home changed" and "something starts using the home" — which is a launch. So
512	a change to a home's units is recorded, and the next launch **refuses** until
513	somebody has read it.
514	
515	### The operator-visible contract
516	
517	- The refusal is **exit 8**, before anything is spawned, with a report of what
518	  moved. A gate that fired after the launch would have already failed to gate.
519	- Bare `home drift` prints the pending change; `home drift --ack` clears it and
520	  the next launch proceeds. `--ack-drift` on a single `skill-manager exec`
521	  acknowledges in passing. Run them through the home's own
522	  `bin/cli/skill-manager`, not a bare `skill-manager` — same reason every remedy
523	  on this page names a resolved path.
524	- Acknowledgement is the **only** thing that retires it. Re-recording a digest
525	  does not: the record is a fact about a change that happened, not a statement
526	  about whether the home is currently self-consistent.
527	- The launcher shims (`bin/launch/{claude,codex,gemini}`) take the gated path,
528	  deliberately. `bootstrap-home.sh`'s own internal `exec` calls pass
529	  `--ack-drift`, so **the bootstrap verifying a home cannot tell you whether the
530	  operator's next command will be refused**.
531	
532	### When a freshly provisioned worktree hits it
533	
534	Measured on a disposable fixture: a worktree cloned from a project home whose
535	content had moved since that home last recorded a digest comes up with a pending
536	record, and `skill-manager exec --home <wt>/.skill-manager -- …` exits 8 with
537	`refusing to launch: … changed and the change has not been read.` Cloned from a
538	home whose digest was current, the same sequence exits 0.
539	
540	"Content moved since the last recorded digest" is the ordinary state of a home
541	anyone is working in, so **expect the gate on a new worktree and do not read it
542	as a broken bootstrap**. Do not, however, encode "always" into a checklist: the
543	gate is a function of the source home's recorded state, both outcomes are
544	correct, and the exact conditions are `skill-manager`'s to change. Read the
545	report, acknowledge it, launch.

547	## `propagate.sh` and skill push-back are different flows
548	
549	Confusing them loses work. They move different things in different directions.
550	
551	| | `propagate.sh` | Skill push-back |
552	|---|---|---|
553	| What moves | A **parent** change: the diff you committed to the integration feature branch | A **skill** change: an edit an agent made to a unit inside its own home |
554	| From | The integration repo's merged feature branch | `<checkout>/.skill-manager/skills/<unit>/` |
555	| To | Each affected constituent's own repo: `feature/<TICKET>` + MR + one tracking issue | That skill's own repo, trunk-style, via `skill-manager project sync` (see the skill-manager skill and the skt plugin's unit-authoring skill) |
556	| Trigger | You merged a cross-repo change | An agent improved a skill while using it |
557	| Ignores the other's state | Yes — it fans out the parent diff and knows nothing about homes | Yes — it pushes a unit and knows nothing about the parent branch |
558	
559	A skill's files inside a home are **not** part of the parent diff: the home is
560	gitignored, so `git add -A` in the worktree never sees them and `propagate.sh`
561	can never carry them. If an agent edits a skill in its home and you only run
562	`propagate.sh`, the edit is not published anywhere — and `git worktree remove`
563	then deletes it. **Push back before teardown.** `close-change.sh` enforces the
564	first, weaker half of that (the edit reaches the *project home*) and will not
565	let a bare removal skip it; getting the edit to the skill's own repo is still
566	this push-back flow, and still yours to run.
567	
568	**And it now says so at the moment it matters.** A successful close prints a
569	`HOME-WORK` key naming the project home the work reached, and `wt close` carries
570	it onto its one line as `push skill edits from there`. That is why it is printed
571	at teardown rather than documented only here: the teardown is exactly when the
572	obligation becomes invisible — the worktree home is deleted, the loss appears in
573	no diff, and until this key existed nothing in the workflow mentioned it
574	(git-integration-skill#8). Note the direction too: push from the **main
575	checkout**. From a worktree the skill's upstream is the wrong target, because
576	the copy of the skill that holds the edit lives in the home being removed.
577	
578	The reverse mistake is just as bad: a skill lives in its own repo, so editing
579	its copy under `constituents/<skill>/` and propagating that is the *parent*
580	flow, and it is the right one when you are changing the skill as a constituent
581	of this repo. Decide which artifact you changed — a repo's files, or a unit
582	inside a home — and use the matching flow.
583	
584	## Policy: `live` and `frozen`
585	
586	`bootstrap-home.sh` declares `live` by default: the home may be synced,
587	upgraded, and pushed back from. `--policy frozen` declares the opposite, for a
588	home whose contents are evidence (an experiment run, a bisect checkpoint).
589	
590	A home that is **already frozen is never modified** — not re-shimmed, not
591	re-described, not re-baselined — and `bootstrap-home.sh` reports the skip
592	instead of "repairing" it. Clone a frozen home to get a live copy; the original
593	stays as it was.

595	## Teardown, including at epic close
596	
597	Tear a worktree down with `close-change.sh`, never with a bare
598	`git worktree remove`:
599	
600	```bash
601	# The gate runs BEFORE anything is deleted.
602	"${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/close-change.sh" TICKET-123
603	
604	# At epic close, list what is left and close each one deliberately.
605	git -C <repo-root> worktree list
606	```
607	
608	`close-change.sh` runs
609	
610	```bash
611	skill-manager home close-out --home <wt>/.skill-manager \
612	                             --into <main-working-tree>/.skill-manager --json
613	```
614	
615	`--into` is the project home the worktree's own home was **cloned from** — the
616	main working tree's, resolved by the same `project_home` helper
617	`bootstrap-home.sh` uses, so where the operator happens to be standing cannot
618	change the answer. It used to be `<checkout_root>/.skill-manager`, i.e. `$PWD`'s
619	nearest git toplevel, which from inside a sibling worktree named *that*
620	worktree's home.
621	
622	Every remedy names a **resolved CLI path**, not a bare `skill-manager`. A bare
623	`skill-manager` on a machine with an older release first on PATH exits 2 for the
624	operator who copy-pastes it, and that is the machine this was found on.
625	
626	The substitution happens in **one** place — `HomeCloseOut` builds the string and
627	names the CLI through `HomeDescriptor.resolveCli`, so `--json` and
628	`home close-out`'s own human output say the same thing. `close-change.sh`
629	renders the remedy verbatim and contributes only the *environment* that
630	resolution runs in.
631	
632	It used to rewrite the string with a regex instead, and that was wrong twice: it
633	fixed only the `--json` consumer, and its token boundary matched inside
634	`skill-manager.toml` — the manifest every unit has, so the most likely conflicted
635	file there is — turning the operator's conflict list into a path in a different
636	repository. `scripts/selftest.sh` now asserts the remedy's **tail**, not just its
637	first token.
638	
639	#### That environment is decided per candidate, and this is where it bit
640	
641	`resolveCli`'s rules are, in order: `$SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`; the running process's
642	own command, when it looks like a launcher (a jbang/JVM process does not);
643	`<store>/bin/cli/skill-manager`; then a bare `skill-manager` off `PATH`. So when
644	`pick_cli` answers with a checkout's or the integration parent's launcher, the
645	export is what keeps a remedy off that last rule — and a bare `skill-manager`
646	here is the released 0.19.2, which exits 2 for whoever copy-pastes it.
647	
648	For a while this page said the export *was* the script's contribution, full
649	stop. That stopped being true the moment `home shims` began writing a pin that
650	honours the same variable: `pick_cli`'s **preferred** candidate is the home's
651	own pin, and
652	
653	```bash
654	SKILL_MANAGER_CLI="$CLI" "$CLI" home close-out …      # WRONG when $CLI is a pin
655	```
656	
657	tells that pin to exec itself, forever. Measured on the epic #2 pilot: 7:03 of
658	CPU over 13:06 of wall clock from one teardown, silently — a teardown that hangs
659	is indistinguishable from a teardown that is slow, which on a fan-out means it
660	is indistinguishable from progress.
661	
662	Neither change was wrong on its own. `home shims` was right to take ownership of
663	the pin; the script was simply still exporting from the era when it owned the
664	pin. They only met at the moment the pin started honouring the variable.
665	
666	So `close-change.sh` now exports **only** to a candidate that does not resolve
667	itself through `$SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`, scrubs an inherited value for one that
668	does, and applies the same rule to its capability *probes* — with the variable
669	already set in an agent's environment, the hang landed inside `pick_cli`, before
670	the script had printed which CLI it was even trying. See
671	[the pin section](#the-pin-resolves-itself-through-skill_manager_cli-so-do-not-point-that-at-it)
672	for the predicate and why it reads the candidate's bytes rather than its path.
673	
674	`selftest.sh` covers it under a hard time bound, because the regression's
675	signature is silence: an unbounded check against it does not go red, it goes
676	away. That section is also the only one that runs with `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`
677	**unset** — with it set, `pick_cli` returns it from the first branch and a home's
678	own pin is never reached, which is how 26 green checks sat on top of this.
679	
680	and **refuses to remove the worktree** (exit 4) while that verdict is non-zero,
681	printing every blocking unit and the exact command that clears it. Run the
682	remedy, re-run the script, and the removal proceeds.
683	
684	### Project plugin lifecycle callback
685	
686	A clean home does not prove external state has been released. A plugin that
687	owns worktree-lifetime state may install one executable in the project home:
688	
689	```text
690	<project-home>/plugins/<plugin>/lifecycle/worktree-pre-remove
691	```
692	
693	`close-change.sh` discovers those executables from the **project home**, in
694	stable bytewise plugin-name order. That location is intentional: it survives
695	the worktree removal, covers a `--no-home` worktree, and is the destination the
696	home gate has already reconciled. It invokes the executable as:
697	
698	```bash
699	worktree-pre-remove check \
700	  --worktree <absolute-worktree> \
701	  --project-root <absolute-main-checkout> \
702	  --project-home <absolute-project-home> \
703	  --worktree-home <absolute-worktree-home>
704	
705	worktree-pre-remove release <same flags>
706	```
707	
708	`check` is read-only and runs on `--dry-run`. `release` runs only after the
709	home gate and every local removal precondition have passed, immediately before
710	`git worktree remove`. The callback locates its own config beneath
711	`--project-home`; this generic lifecycle does not interpret plugin data.
712	
713	Each callback is bounded to 30 seconds and its diagnostic streams to 16 KiB.
714	A non-zero exit or timeout refuses with exit 4 and preserves the worktree.
715	`--force` does not bypass this refusal: that flag names a deliberate discard of
716	home bytes, while an unreleased external binding is still live state. There is
717	an unavoidable narrow `release` → `git worktree remove` failure window; putting
718	release after every other local check is the smallest honest local transaction.
719	
720	Why a script rather than a rule: `git worktree remove` succeeds with a home
721	inside it because the home is ignored, not untracked — which is also why the
722	ignore rules matter. It deletes the home **without asking**, and it succeeds
723	exactly as quietly whether the home held a week of skill edits or nothing.
724	Because the home is gitignored, the loss shows up in no diff, so "push back
725	before teardown" was a discipline that failed silently the first time anyone
726	forgot. The gate makes it a mechanism.
727	
728	### The override, and why it exists
729	
730	```bash
731	"${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/close-change.sh" TICKET-123 --force
732	```
733	
734	`--force` still runs the gate and still prints the blockers; it only declines to
735	stop, and it says plainly that the work is being discarded. It exists because a
736	gate with no escape hatch does not stop the operator who genuinely wants to
737	throw a spike away — it routes them to `rm -rf` or `git worktree remove --force`
738	by hand, which skips this check *and* every other one. A named, loud override is
739	safer than an improvised one. It does not override a project plugin lifecycle
740	callback failure.
741	
742	### How it degrades
743	
744	The rule is: proceed only when the gate has actually established there is
745	nothing to lose.
746	
747	| Situation | What close-change.sh does | Why |
748	|---|---|---|
749	| Worktree has **no home** (`--no-home`) | Removes it, saying the gate was skipped | Absence of a home really is proof there is no home-resident work |
750	| **No `skill-manager` with `close-out`** on `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI`, the home's `bin/cli`, the checkout, the enclosing integration repo, or PATH | **Refuses** | Absence of the tool is absence of *proof*, which is not the same thing. A gate that opens when it cannot check is not a gate |
751	| **Project home missing** (`--into` does not exist) | **Refuses** | The work has nowhere to go and there is nothing to compare against |
752	| Gate reports blockers | **Refuses**, printing each remedy | The case the gate exists for |
753	| Project plugin lifecycle callback fails or times out | **Refuses even with `--force`** | External state was not proven released; deleting local bytes cannot repair that |
754	
755	The capability probe reads the CLI's help **text**, not its exit status, for the
756	same measured reason `bootstrap-home.sh` does: the released 0.19.2 answers
757	`home close-out --help` by printing top-level usage and **exiting 0**. A
758	status-only probe would accept a CLI with no `close-out` at all and the teardown
759	would sail past a gate that never ran.
760	
761	### Reconciling is not publishing
762	
763	The gate's remedy (`home sync … --merge`) moves the work into the **project
764	home**, which is what stops the teardown destroying it. That is not the same as
765	getting the edit back to the skill's own repository — for that, see the
766	push-back flow in the table above. Clearing the gate makes the edit survive the
767	worktree; it does not make it survive the machine.
768	
769	The global `~/.skill-manager` is never a teardown target. Nothing in this flow
770	writes it; `bootstrap-home.sh` refuses outright if a target home would resolve
771	to it.

773	## Ignoring the homes
774	
775	### What actually keeps the tree clean
776	
777	**`bootstrap-home.sh` writes a per-checkout rule into `$GIT_COMMON_DIR/info/exclude`.**
778	That is the mechanism. It is not the `.gitignore` list below, and for a long time
779	this page said it was.
780	
781	The script does not work from a list. It records the untracked top-level entries
782	before it does anything, records them again afterwards, and excludes the
783	difference — plus any untracked entry whose name the home machinery owns
784	(`.claude*`, `.codex*`, `.gemini*`, `.skill-manager*`, read from the home's own
785	descriptor, never from a literal list in the script). Whatever a run creates is
786	that run's to account for, **whatever it is called**. The second rule is what
787	covers the ordinary re-run, where an earlier `install` / `sync` /
788	`project resolve` left a file behind before the script started.
789	
790	It goes in the exclude file rather than in `.gitignore` because `.gitignore` is
791	**tracked**: appending to it makes the tree dirty a different way — one modified
792	file instead of one untracked one — and `wt new` refuses either way until someone
793	commits it. Making the script commit was built and measured, and the cost decided
794	against it: **a repo nobody can commit to could not get a home.** Read-only
795	checkouts, CI, and vendored third-party constituents are not edge cases in an
796	integration repo, they are most of it. (Measured on the way past: three
797	`selftest.sh` fixtures carried no `.gitignore` at all, and the suite went to
798	71 passed / 44 failed until each was onboarded by hand. That is first contact for
799	a real user.)
800	
801	Reading the exclude file from the **common** dir means one write covers the main
802	tree and every linked worktree, and the `/`-anchored rules apply at each worktree
803	root separately — which is what is wanted, since every worktree gets its own home.
804	
805	### The cost, said out loud
806	
807	**A rule in `info/exclude` is invisible to everyone else.** It makes the checkout
808	in hand clean and does nothing for a teammate, a CI job, or a fresh clone — they
809	all still see `?? .skill-manager` and friends. It also lives where no review will
810	ever see it.
811	
812	And because it leaves a tree *exactly* as clean as a `.gitignore` rule does,
813	`git status` cannot tell the two apart. Only `git check-ignore -v` names the
814	source, which is why `selftest.sh` asserts the source by name rather than
815	asserting "clean" — a check that only asserted cleanliness would pass under
816	either mechanism and prove nothing about which one ran.
817	
818	### Recommended, not required: commit the rules too
819	
820	A repo whose contributors all want a clean tree should **also** carry these in a
821	tracked `.gitignore`. Put them at the **parent root** — never in a file inside a
822	constituent (`INTEGRATION.md` rule 2):
823	
824	```gitignore
825	/.skill-manager/
826	/.claude/
827	/.claude.json
828	/.codex/
829	/.gemini/
830	constituents/*/.skill-manager/
831	constituents/*/.claude/
832	constituents/*/.claude.json
833	constituents/*/.codex/
834	constituents/*/.gemini/
835	```
836	
837	This is a **recommendation**. Nothing depends on it: `bootstrap-home.sh` does not
838	read this list, does not check it, and does not refuse without it. The benefit is
839	that a fresh clone is clean *before* anyone runs a bootstrap, and that the rule is
840	visible in review. When a rule here already covers a path, the bootstrap adds
841	nothing for it — git never reports an ignored path as untracked, so it never
842	reaches the exclude loop, and the two mechanisms compose rather than duplicate.
843	
844	`/.claude.json` is in the list because `/.claude/` does not match it, and because
845	skill-manager builds **before 0.20.0** wrote claude's MCP registration to
846	`<root>/.claude.json`, beside the agent directory rather than inside it — which
847	left `?? .claude.json` in `git status` and made `wt new` refuse a freshly
848	onboarded repo. **That is fixed in the product.** Measured against
849	`skill-manager 0.20.0+g651691a`: the registration goes to
850	`<root>/.claude/.claude.json` (with a `.claude.json.lock` beside it), both already
851	covered by `/.claude/`, and a bootstrap + install now leaves only
852	`.skill-manager/`, `.claude/`, `.codex/` and `.gemini/` at a checkout root. The
853	rule is kept because older builds are still in the field and it costs nothing —
854	not because the defect is current.
855	
856	That measurement is also the reason none of this is enumerated anywhere: the list
857	was right until the product moved the file, and it will be wrong again the next
858	time something new appears at a checkout root. The bootstrap will report that one;
859	a list will not.
860	
861	If you do add them, **prove them** — a constituent's own `.gitignore` is more
862	specific than the root's and a negated rule in it wins:
863	
864	```bash
865	git check-ignore -v .skill-manager/home.runtime.json
866	for d in constituents/*/; do git check-ignore -v "$d.skill-manager/x" || echo "NOT IGNORED: $d"; done
867	```
868	
869	Every path must be reported as ignored. **Read which file `-v` names**, because
870	that is the difference between a rule the repo carries and a rule only this clone
871	has: `.gitignore` (or a constituent's own, which just means it already agrees)
872	means everyone gets it; `.git/info/exclude` means the bootstrap put it there and
873	nobody else has it. What must never happen is a path reported as not ignored, or
874	a home showing up in `git status`: committing a home would put another machine's
875	absolute paths, and a copy of every installed unit, into the parent repo.
876	
877	**These rules cover a home, not a worktree.** A ticket worktree of a nested
878	integration repo or of a constituent is a whole checkout, and no ignore rule in
879	the parent can safely name it: a glob matching
880	`constituents/meta-orchestrator-CO2` also matches `constituents/deploy-helm`.
881	Worse, the worktree's `.git` is a file, so a parent `git add -A` stages it as a
882	gitlink rather than as files. That is why `new-change.sh` puts such worktrees
883	**outside** the outermost integration repo instead — see
884	`references/worktrees.md`. Nothing needs adding to the parent's `.gitignore`
885	for it.
886	
887	## Bootstrapping the repo that ships the bootstrap
888	
889	An integration repo that contains the CLI or the skill implementing this
890	mechanism has a genuine circular dependency the first time: the worktree that
891	installs the hook must itself be created the old way (`git worktree add`) and
892	have its home bootstrapped by hand inside it. That is expected once, not a bug
893	to chase.
894	
895	Two measured consequences worth knowing before you rely on the in-repo copy:
896	
897	- **A parent worktree carries the parent's *committed snapshot* of a
898	  constituent**, not that constituent's current branch. On this repo the
899	  snapshot's `skill-manager` had no `home` command at all while the main tree's
900	  working copy did, so a worktree could not bootstrap from the repo's own CLI
901	  until the snapshot was refreshed. Pin `SKILL_MANAGER_CLI` in the meantime — at
902	  a real `skill-manager` **launcher**, never at a home's `bin/cli/skill-manager`
903	  shim, which resolves itself through that same variable and would exec itself
904	  forever.
905	- **`new-change.sh` requires a clean parent tree**, and a parent mid-epic is
906	  often dirty with constituent drift. Then the worktree is created by hand and
907	  `bootstrap-home.sh --root <wt>` run against it — the same two steps the hook
908	  performs, in the same order.
909	
910	## Onboarding any integration repo
911	
912	1. Onboard the repo the ordinary way (`references/onboarding.md`).
913	2. Add the ignore rules above to the parent root `.gitignore`, then verify with
914	   `git check-ignore -v`.
915	3. Write a `skill-project.toml` at the root declaring the units this repo's
916	   agents need. It is portable intent — the realized state is the home.
917	4. Give the main tree its home, once:
918	   `${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/bootstrap-home.sh --root <repo>`.
919	   This is the whole step. It is also exactly the `fix:` line `wt new` prints, in
920	   full and already absolute, when it meets a repository with no home — so an
921	   agent that never read this page arrives at the same command.
922	5. *Optional convenience:* copy this skill's `scripts/agent-home.sh` (the
923	   locator) into the repo's own `scripts/` so a human can type
924	   `scripts/agent-home.sh` instead of the path in step 4:
925	   `cp ${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/agent-home.sh scripts/`.
926	   Skip it freely — nothing downstream requires the copy, and an agent should
927	   never have to check whether a given repo has one.
928	6. From then on, `new-change.sh` gives every worktree its own home. Nothing to
929	   remember and nothing to **export** — which is a statement about the
930	   environment, not a promise that the first launch will proceed. Expect the
931	   change-awareness gate (exit 8) on a new worktree and clear it with
932	   bare `skill-manager home drift`, then the same command plus `--ack`; see
